tekamolo.title: TeKaMoLo
tekamolo.lead: A useful order for the middle field — not an iron law.

detail.label: The base order

runs.t: Ich fahre heute wegen des Wetters mit dem Bus zur Arbeit

comment: English reshuffles the same facts: “Because of the weather, I’m taking the bus to work today” — time comes last.

detail.label: The predicted error
comment: Calquing the English order — place before time — is the classic English-speaker slip.

detail.label: Why it is not a law
runs: Emphasis, pronouns and definiteness can reorder the middle field. Treat TeKaMoLo as the safe default while you are unsure.

particles.title: Particles: breakdown
particles.lead: Mid-field position — usually right after the verb or the subject.

detail.label: doch
comment: “But it is late, you know”: pushes back against what the other person knows or has just said.

detail.label: ja
comment: “That’s clear, after all”: obvious to both of you — no proof needed.

detail.label: denn
comment: “So what’s your name, then?”: friendly interest, not “why”. Not the conjunction denn — that one lives in Clauses.

detail.label: mal
comment: “Come here a sec”: softens a request into a nudge.

detail.label: schon / gar
comment: “True, I suppose” (concession) · “not hard at all” (intensifier — almost always with nicht).

detail.label: wohl
comment: “probably”: a cautious guess, no certainty.

detail.label: Position
comment: After the finite verb or the subject, before the rest — English carries the same nuance with stress: “I did NOT say anything.”

detail.label: e→i stays, umlaut goes
comment: The vowel change survives; the umlaut disappears in the command.

detail.label: -t/-d stems
comment: Insert -e-. Pure form learning — English has no parallel here.

detail.label: sein
comment: The exception — and the form you will actually use with strangers: “Be quiet, please.”

detail.label: ihr / Sie
comment: Sie keeps its place after the verb — a command shape English simply does not have.

detail.label: als
runs: One specific time in the past:
comment: ≈ “when I was a child” — one occasion, closed and gone.

detail.label: wenn

runs.t: Wenn ich Zeit habe, komme ich.

comment: ≈ “when(ever) I have time, I’ll come.”

detail.label: English “if”
comment: English “if” covers both jobs; German splits them — wenn vs ob.

obwohl.title: obwohl vs trotzdem
obwohl.lead: Both give a contrast, but they build the sentence differently.

detail.label: trotzdem
runs: Adverb in the main clause → V2: Es regnet.
comment: The same line English draws between “nevertheless” and “although”.

coordinators.title: weil vs denn
coordinators.lead: Both = “because”, but the word order is different.

detail.label: denn
comment: After denn the normal order stays — like after

sondern.title: sondern vs aber
sondern.lead: After a negation (nicht, kein) the correction takes sondern — “not A, but B”. A plain contrast without a correction — aber.

detail.label: sondern — the correction
comment: “not from Bucharest but from Deva”: first negate, then correct to the other option.

detail.label: aber — plain “but”
comment: Both facts stand; nothing is corrected. Error:

comment.t: Er mag keinen Fisch, aber Fleisch

comment: (“not fish but meat”).

detail.label: nicht nur …, sondern auch
comment: “not only German but also English.”

detail.label: Word order
runs: — normal word order follows: …, sondern sie

detail.label: The trigger
runs: English “but” covers both jobs too. The German trigger: a
in front of the corrected part → sondern.
comment: “not A, but B” → sondern; plain “but” → aber.

um-damit.title: um … zu vs damit
um-damit.lead: English makes the same split: in order to vs so that.

detail.label: um … zu
runs: Same subject on both sides: Ich lerne,
comment: ≈ “I’m learning in order to work in Germany.”

detail.label: damit
runs: A full subordinate clause — the subjects differ: Ich spreche langsam,
comment: ≈ “I speak slowly so that you understand me.”

detail.label: zu with separable verbs
comment: The prefix jumps in front of zu: “Es ist schwer, früh
” ≈ “It’s hard to get up early.”

relative.title: Relative clauses
relative.lead: The relative pronoun is the definite article in disguise: gender and number from the noun, case from its role inside the clause.

detail.label: Nominativ inside
comment: The pronoun is the subject: Wer arbeitet? — der.

detail.label: Akkusativ inside
comment: The pronoun is the object: Wen kenne ich? — den.

detail.label: Dativ inside
comment: The receiver: Wem helfe ich? — dem.

detail.label: Genitiv inside
comment: “whose” (masc./neut.);
for fem./plural.

linking-adverbs.title: Linking adverbs: the details
linking-adverbs.lead: Position 1, verb right after: Deshalb blieben wir…

detail.label: deshalb / deswegen
comment: “so / that’s why”: the cause stands in the first sentence.

detail.label: trotzdem vs obwohl
runs: es regnete. — conjunction, verb to the end.
comment: The same line English draws between “nevertheless” and “although”. “Trotzdem, dass…” is colloquial; standard is obwohl.

detail.label: allerdings
comment: “though / however”: a soft contrast.

detail.label: außerdem
comment: “besides”: one more thing on the pile.

detail.label: währenddessen
comment: “meanwhile”: at the same time.

detail.label: Position
runs: : normal order after it — see weil vs denn.
